questions.p: Kevin, 34, is stabbed in the right side of his back. His arms are normal. His right leg is weak, with hyperactive reflexes and an extensor plantar response. Vibration and proprioception are lost in the right leg. Pain and temperature are lost in the left leg. Where is the lesion?
o: Right half of the thoracic cord
Left half of the thoracic cord
Right half of the cervical cord
questions.e:
A is correct. Dorsal columns run ipsilateral in the cord, so right vibration loss points to the right side. Spinothalamic tracts cross at entry, so pain loss is contralateral. UMN signs in a leg with normal arms place it in the thoracic cord.
B: Lesions below L1 give LMN signs, with reduced reflexes and flexor plantars.
C: A left lesion would cause left leg weakness and left vibration loss.
D: A cervical lesion would also affect the arms.
High yield: UMN: brain, brainstem, cord. LMN: anterior horn, root, nerve, NMJ, muscle.

questions.p: Linda, 52, notices complete loss of vision in her left eye over a few days. With the left eye covered, her right eye has full visual fields. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.e:
D is correct. Each eye's information travels in its own optic nerve until the chiasm. A lesion before the chiasm affects one eye only.
A: An occipital lesion also affects the same hemifield in both eyes, as in your Week 7 quiz.
B: Left hemifield information from each eye runs in the right optic tract, so a tract lesion affects both eyes.
C: Behind the optic nerve, fibres from both eyes travel together, so field loss would involve both eyes.
High yield: Retina, optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, LGN, optic radiation, visual cortex.

questions.p: During a periodic health exam, Mr. Novak, 82, has several findings noted. Which one is best explained by normal aging rather than disease?
o: Memory loss that stops him managing finances
A maximal exercise heart rate of about 120 bpm
Fasting glucose of 7.4 mmol/L on two occasions
Three falls in 6 months while walking indoors
questions.e:
B is correct. Maximal heart rate falls with age, estimated as 200 minus age. For 82, that is about 118 bpm. Age-related changes are universal.
A: Cognitive loss that impairs independence is dementia.
C: FPG of 7.0 mmol/L or more is in the diabetes range.
D: Falls are almost always multifactorial and need assessment.
High yield: Age-related change is universal. Disease-related change is not.

questions.p: During a MoCA, Mrs. Ibrahim names the camel and lion but calls the rhinoceros a hippo. On verbal fluency she produces 12 words in 60 seconds. For abstraction, she says a train and bicycle both have wheels, and a watch and ruler are both used to measure. How many points does she earn across these three sections combined?
questions.e:
C is correct. Naming: camel and lion score, hippo does not (2). Fluency: 11 or more words scores 1. Abstraction: has wheels scores 0, used to measure scores 1. Total 4.
A: 6 credits the hippo and the wheels answer.
B: 3 misses the fluency point, since 12 clears the threshold of 11.
D: 5 credits the concrete answer about wheels.
High yield: Abstraction needs the category (means of transportation, measuring instruments).

questions.p: Mr. Dubois, 84, is on day 2 after hip fracture repair. He is drowsy and drifts off mid-sentence. He states his age and date of birth correctly but gives the wrong year and cannot name the hospital. He lists five months backwards before stopping. His daughter says he was sharp last week. What is his 4-AT score and interpretation?
questions.e:
C is correct. Alertness clearly abnormal = 4. AMT4 with 2 mistakes = 2. Fewer than 7 months = 1. Acute change = 4. Total 11. A score of 4 or more indicates possible delirium.
A: 7 drops the 4 points for clearly abnormal alertness.
B: 1-3 indicates possible cognitive impairment, which fits an alert patient without acute change.
D: The 4-AT screens for delirium, and the acute change argues against dementia.
High yield: Do not use the MoCA in suspected delirium. Use the 4-AT.

questions.p: Mrs. Chen, 76, and her son report 18 months of misplacing items and repeating questions. Her MoCA is 22/30 with deficits mainly in delayed recall. She still pays her bills, fills her own pill organizer, cooks full meals and drives without incident. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.e:
B is correct. She has a subjective change and an objective deficit, but daily functioning is preserved. That is MCI.
A: Normal aging gives a subjective change without an objective deficit.
C: Dementia needs deficits that interfere with independence in everyday activities.
D: Delirium is acute and fluctuating, not an 18-month course.
High yield: MCI converts to dementia at about 10% per year.

questions.p: Mrs. Rossi, 88, has mild dementia. On the second night of a hospital stay for cellulitis she becomes acutely confused and agitated. She was given an antihistamine for sleep the night before. A bladder scan shows 650 mL of retained urine. Which explanation fits best?
o: Dementia progression from the hospital stay
Delirium from a drug and urinary retention
questions.e:
B is correct. An acute change with triggers is delirium. Antihistamines (drugs) and urinary retention (pee) are both DIMESPPP precipitants, and dementia is a risk factor.
A: Dementia progresses over months to years.
C: Depression has an insidious onset over weeks to months.
D: Antipsychotics are not first choice for behavioural symptoms, and a reversible cause is present.
High yield: Delirium is acute, fluctuating and reversible.

questions.p: A family physician sorts four referrals for a dementia workup. None of the patients takes anticoagulants, has a cancer history or shows focal neurologic signs. Which patient meets an indication for neuroimaging?
o: A 57-year-old with 14 months of memory decline
A 76-year-old with 5 years of gradual decline
An 80-year-old with 4 years of slow memory decline
A 79-year-old whose MoCA fell 2 points in 2 years
questions.e:
A is correct. Age under 60 and dementia of short duration (under 2 years) are both abnormal presentations that call for neuroimaging.
B: Gradual 5-year decline without focal signs has no listed indication.
C: Slow decline over 4 years at 80 is not an abnormal presentation.
D: A small, gradual MoCA drop is not rapid decline over 1-2 months.
High yield: BRAIN: bleeding risk, abnormal presentation, intracranial lesion, normal pressure hydrocephalus.

questions.p: Mrs. Patel, 81, is brought in by her daughter for 2 months of fatigue, apathy and generalized weakness. ECG shows new atrial fibrillation. She denies heat intolerance, palpitations or irritability. Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
questions.e:
B is correct. Hyperthyroidism in older adults presents atypically with new atrial fibrillation, generalized weakness, apathy, fatigue and delirium.
A: Depression explains apathy but not new atrial fibrillation.
C: Rapid AF presents atypically with anorexia, fatigue and falls, but leaves the new AF unexplained.
D: Atypical MI presents with abdominal pain, nausea, functional decline or delirium.
High yield: Geriatric syndromes: weakness, falls, delirium, incontinence, functional decline, weight loss.

questions.p: Mr. Okafor, 79, lives alone. He bathes, dresses and feeds himself without help. Over the past year his daughter has taken over his grocery shopping and housework because he cannot walk far alone, and he no longer prepares meals. Which Clinical Frailty Scale score fits best?
questions.e:
A is correct. CFS 5 needs help in high order IADLs such as shopping, walking alone, meal preparation and housework. His personal care is independent.
B: CFS 4 is not dependent on others for daily help.
C: CFS 6 needs help with all outside activities and with bathing.
D: CFS 7 is complete dependence for personal care.
High yield: Bathing help separates CFS 6 from 5.

questions.p: Mr. Tremblay, 71, has a 20 pack-year smoking history and quit 25 years ago. He feels well. At his periodic health encounter, which screening test is indicated?
o: Annual low-dose CT scan of the chest
Serum PSA test every 2 to 4 years
questions.e:
B is correct. Men 65-80 get one-time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
A: Lung screening needs 30 pack-years and quitting under 15 years ago.
C: Thyroid screening is not recommended when asymptomatic.
D: PSA screening is not recommended in the older adult PHE.
High yield: Also due: colorectal screening to 74, Pneumovax at 65+.

questions.p: A geriatrics tutor lists factors linked to living past 100. Which of the following is NOT one of the factors associated with centenarians?
o: A first-degree relative who lived to an advanced age
Naturally having a child after age 40
A non-smoking history in a lean male
questions.e:
D is correct. Centenarians tend to show low neuroticism and high extraversion, the reverse of this option.
A: A first-degree relative of advanced age is a factor, as in your Week 7 quiz.
B: Women who naturally have a child after 40 are listed.
C: Lean males with no smoking history are listed.
High yield: Healthy aging: no smoking, Mediterranean diet, BMI 24-30, 7-8 hours of sleep, limited alcohol, exercise, social engagement.

questions.p: Mrs. Duval, 83, fell at home twice this month. Her review notes poor vision, leg weakness, a new sleeping pill, a loose hallway carpet and a glass of wine each night. Which pair are both intrinsic causes of falls?
o: Loose carpet and the sleeping pill
questions.e:
A is correct. Intrinsic causes include poor balance, weakness, chronic illness, visual and cognitive impairment. Medications, alcohol and loose carpets are extrinsic.
B: Both are extrinsic causes.
C: The loose carpet is extrinsic.
D: Alcohol is extrinsic.
High yield: Falls are almost always multifactorial. Never call one mechanical.

questions.p: Mr. Ali, 80, dresses, eats, walks, uses the toilet and bathes on his own. Over the past year his daughter has taken over paying his bills and buying his groceries. Which functional domain and items are affected?
questions.e:
C is correct. IADLs follow SHAFT: shopping, housework, accounting, food preparation, telephone. Bills (accounting) and groceries (shopping) are IADLs.
A: Telephone and food preparation are IADLs but are not described as affected.
B: He walks and toilets on his own.
D: He manages hygiene and dressing on his own.
High yield: ADLs follow DEATH: dressing, eating, ambulating, toileting, hygiene.

questions.p: Mrs. Kim, 78, lists amoxicillin as an allergy in her medication history. On questioning, she had loose stools starting on day 5 of a course, with no rash, swelling or breathing trouble. How is this reaction best classified?
o: Drug intolerance, from a gut microbiome change
Type-1 hypersensitivity allergy to the drug class
Anaphylaxis from the first few doses
questions.e:
A is correct. Drug intolerances are usually caused by changes in the gut microbiome and include nausea, diarrhea and delirium. Allergies are type-1 hypersensitivity reactions that range from rash to anaphylaxis and start after the first few doses.
B: A type-1 allergy produces rash or anaphylaxis, not isolated diarrhea.
C: Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergy with no features here.
D: Pseudoallergic reactions are anaphylactoid, as after radiocontrast media.
High yield: Your Week 7 quiz asked the reverse: wheezing and hypotension mean true allergy.

questions.p: Mr. Grant, 81, tells you he is fine and has no problems at home. His MoCA is 19/30, and his wife, sitting beside him, looks worried and shakes her head. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Take a collateral history from his wife
Refer him directly for brain neuroimaging
Accept his account as the full history
questions.e:
A is correct. Collateral history matters in patients with cognitive problems, unintentional minimization and difficulties with insight. His wife knows him well.
B: Imaging needs a specific indication, and the history is not yet complete.
C: His cognitive impairment and minimization make his account incomplete.
D: Delaying review misses current safety and function concerns.
High yield: Collateral source: someone who knows the patient well, such as a spouse, child, caregiver or friend.

questions.p: Mr. Walsh, 77, is a white man who lives alone since his wife died last year. He has chronic back pain and has been drinking more. He screens positive for depression and admits to thoughts of death. Which factor is the strongest predictor of the course of his suicidal ideation?
questions.e:
D is correct. Each of these is a suicide risk factor in older adults, but severity of depression is the strongest predictor of the course of suicidal ideation.
A: Pain and disability are risk factors, not the strongest predictor.
B: Living alone and recent loss are risk factors, not the strongest predictor.
C: Demographics are risk factors, not the strongest predictor.
High yield: Suicide is almost twice as frequent in older adults and more lethal.

questions.p: Mrs. Ng, 86, has moderate dementia and lives in long-term care. Staff report she has become withdrawn, eats less and no longer joins activities. Which tool is best suited to screen her for depression?
o: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia
questions.e:
C is correct. The Cornell Scale (19 items) is the depression screen designed for people with dementia.
A: The GDS-15 is a yes/no self-report scale.
B: The 4-AT screens for delirium, not depression.
D: The PHQ-9 is a self-report tool that does not account for dementia.
High yield: Screen everyone over 60 and anyone newly admitted to long-term care for depression.

questions.p: Mr. Fischer, 74, has 18 months of progressive memory loss. You order bloodwork to rule out mimickers of dementia. Which of the following is NOT part of that standard workup?
questions.e:
B is correct. The workup is CBC, TSH, electrolytes, calcium (with albumin), glucose and vitamin B12. Glucose is listed, but HbA1c is not.
A: B12 deficiency is a listed mimicker.
C: TSH screens for thyroid dysfunction.
D: CBC is listed.
E: Calcium with albumin is listed.
High yield: Mimickers: delirium, depression, drugs, metabolic causes such as B12, liver or thyroid dysfunction.

questions.p: Mr. Lopez, 84, has Alzheimer's dementia and lives in a nursing home. Over three days he has become agitated and keeps pacing at night. Which is the most appropriate first step?
o: Start a benzodiazepine for night sleep
Start an antipsychotic to control the agitation
Start an SSRI for behavioural symptoms
Look for triggers such as pain or constipation
questions.e:
D is correct. Non-pharmacologic management of BPSD comes first: look for triggers such as pain, medications, constipation and urinary retention, and use distraction.
A: Benzodiazepines are not first choice for agitation in older adults.
B: Antipsychotics are a last resort and not first choice for BPSD.
C: SSRIs are a pharmacologic option after triggers are addressed.
High yield: DICE: describe, investigate, create a plan, evaluate.

questions.p: Mrs. Bauer, 80, has a Clinical Frailty Scale score of 4. She wants to avoid becoming frail. Which plan best fits the prevention strategies in the notes?
o: Limit her walking to lower her risk of falling at home
Exercise, Mediterranean diet and protein supplements
Weight loss diet to bring BMI below 24
Start a benzodiazepine to improve sleep
questions.e:
B is correct. Non-pharmacologic prevention of frailty includes exercise, avoiding immobility, a Mediterranean diet, protein supplementation and a comprehensive geriatric assessment.
A: Limiting activity promotes immobility, which prevention avoids.
C: Healthy aging targets a BMI of 24-30.
D: Benzodiazepines are high-risk drugs that cause falls and cognitive change.
High yield: Frailty is not the same as comorbidity, disability or aging.

questions.p: Two members of the team caring for Mr. Bell, 85, are described. Member 1 assesses his risk of falls, his need for a gait aid and his fear of falling. Member 2 sets up blister packs for his medications. Who are they, in order?
questions.e:
B is correct. The physiotherapist assesses falls risk, gait aid needs and fear of falling. The pharmacist helps with medication aids such as dosettes or blister packs.
A: The dietitian assesses nutrition and protein needs.
C: The OT assesses function, mobility, cognition and safety at home, not gait aid suitability.
D: The social worker helps with caregiver burden and future planning.
High yield: Speech and language pathology: word-finding and swallowing problems in dementia.

questions.p: Mrs. Taylor, 88, has recently come home from hospital. Her son asks how to arrange OHIP-funded nursing and physiotherapy at her home. Which resource fits, and who is able to make the referral?
o: Parkwood driving program, by family request
Home and Community Care, by the family physician's referral only
Alzheimer Society First Link, by LHIN referral
Home and Community Care, by physician, patient or caregiver
questions.e:
D is correct. Home and Community Care by the LHIN provides OHIP-funded nursing, OT, PT, SW and personal support at home. The physician, patient or caregiver makes the referral.
A: Parkwood assesses driving competency.
B: Referrals are not limited to the physician.
C: First Link offers dementia education and support groups.
High yield: It also coordinates pay-per-service supports such as meal delivery and LTC admission.

questions.p: Ms. Ortiz, 34, has double vision, drooping eyelids and trouble swallowing that worsen over weeks. Her limb reflexes are normal or reduced, plantar responses are flexor and sensation is normal. Where is the lesion?
questions.e:
D is correct. Eyes and swallowing with LMN-type findings and spared sensation localize to the NMJ.
A: A root lesion is limited to one myotome.
B: Muscle disease gives generalized proximal weakness.
C: Multiple nerve lesions involve sensation.
E: The brainstem gives UMN signs such as brisk reflexes and extensor plantars.
High yield: Your mock exam miss: NMJ means eyes and swallowing, not a single myotome.

questions.p: Mr. Brown, 62, struggles to rise from a chair and lift his arms above his head. Weakness is symmetric in the shoulders and hips. Eye movements and swallowing are normal, sensation is normal and plantars are flexor. Where is the lesion?
questions.e:
D is correct. Generalized proximal weakness with spared sensation and no UMN signs localizes to muscle.
A: A cervical cord lesion gives UMN signs in four limbs.
B: A root lesion causes weakness in one myotome.
C: A single nerve lesion is limited to that nerve's distribution.
E: The NMJ typically involves the eyes and swallowing.
High yield: LMN sites: anterior horn cell, root, nerve, NMJ, muscle.

questions.p: Two patients have LMN weakness in one leg. Patient 1's weakness and numbness match the distribution of a single named peripheral nerve. Patient 2's weakness matches a single myotome. Which localization fits each, in order?
o: Single nerve, then anterior horn cell
questions.e:
A is correct. Weakness in the distribution of one nerve localizes to that nerve. Weakness in a single myotome matches the distribution of a root.
B: This reverses the two.
C: Multiple nerves give a wider pattern, and muscle disease is generalized and proximal.
D: A single myotome pattern is the root pattern.
High yield: For LMN lesions, ask whether sensation is affected and what the distribution is.

questions.p: An MRI shows a lesion confined to one region of the spinal cord. The radiology resident reviews cord anatomy. Which statement is correct?
o: The spinal cord ends at L5, with cauda equina below
Cord grey matter carries ascending and descending tracts
Cord grey matter is inside, with white matter tracts outside
Cord white matter holds the neuronal cell bodies
questions.e:
C is correct. The spinal cord has grey matter (neuronal cell bodies) inside and white matter (ascending sensory and descending motor tracts) outside. The brain is the reverse.
A: The cord ends at L1, with the cauda equina (lumbar roots) below L1.
B: The tracts run in the outer white matter.
D: Cell bodies sit in grey matter. White matter holds axon tracts.
High yield: Brain: grey outside, white inside. Cord: grey inside, white outside.

questions.p: A neuroanatomy tutor asks where two sensory pathways cross the midline. Which pairing is correct for the vibration and proprioception pathway, then the pain and temperature pathway, in order?
o: Thalamus, then at entry to the spinal cord
At entry to the spinal cord, then medulla
Medulla for both of the two pathways
Medulla, then at entry to the spinal cord
questions.e:
D is correct. The dorsal column (vibration and proprioception) runs ipsilateral in the dorsal cord and crosses in the medulla. The spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature) crosses at entry to the cord and runs contralateral in the lateral cord.
A: The thalamus is a relay station on both pathways, not the crossing point.
B: This reverses the two tracts.
C: Spinothalamic fibres cross as soon as they enter the cord.
High yield: Sensory pathway: nerves, roots, cord, brainstem, thalamus, white matter, primary sensory cortex.

questions.p: Mr. Haddad, 70, develops sudden weakness of his left arm, left leg and the left side of his face over a few minutes. He has brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response on the left. Where is the lesion?
questions.e:
B is correct. Face involvement with arm and leg weakness (hemibody pattern) places the lesion in the brain. Motor fibres cross in the medullary pyramids, so left-sided weakness comes from the right hemisphere. A hyperacute onset over minutes points to stroke.
A: A cord lesion spares the face, and the left cord affects the left limbs below it without facial weakness.
C: A cord lesion spares the face.
D: The left hemisphere controls the right side of the body.
High yield: Motor cortex plans movement for the contralateral side.

questions.p: Jordan, 22, is rear-ended and hits his neck. He now has weakness in both arms and both legs, hyperactive reflexes in all four limbs and bilateral extensor plantar responses. His face, speech, eye movements and swallowing are normal. Where is the lesion?
questions.e:
B is correct. UMN signs in all four limbs (quadriparesis) with normal cranial nerves localize to the cervical spinal cord.
A: A thoracic lesion causes paraparesis and spares the arms.
C: Brainstem lesions involve cranial nerves, which are normal here.
D: The NMJ gives LMN-type weakness with eye and swallowing involvement.
High yield: Hyperacute onset after trauma fits the trauma category of the time course.

questions.p: Leon, 58, has weak, wasted muscles of his right hand. The examiner sees fasciculations, reduced tendon reflexes and a flexor plantar response, with normal tone. Which localization is LEAST consistent with these findings?
questions.e:
A is correct. Atrophy, fasciculations, reduced reflexes and normal tone are LMN signs. The brainstem is a UMN localization.
B: A peripheral nerve is an LMN site.
C: The anterior horn cell is an LMN site, and fasciculations fit.
D: A spinal root is an LMN site.
High yield: UMN: brain, brainstem, spinal cord. LMN: anterior horn cell, root, nerve, NMJ, muscle.

questions.p: Grace, 64, has 3 weeks of progressive weakness in both legs. Her arms are normal. Her leg muscles are wasted, ankle and knee reflexes are absent and plantar responses are flexor. Where is the lesion?
questions.e:
A is correct. Weakness in both legs (paraparesis) arises in the thoracic cord or the lumbar roots. LMN signs (wasting, absent reflexes, flexor plantars) point below L1, where the cord has ended and only roots remain.
B: A thoracic cord lesion gives UMN signs, as in the 65-year-old in your Week 7 quiz.
C: A cervical lesion weakens all four limbs.
D: NMJ weakness involves the eyes and swallowing.
High yield: Paraparesis plus UMN signs means thoracic cord. Paraparesis plus LMN signs means lumbar roots.

questions.p: Two patients have full strength on testing. Patient 1 overshoots when reaching for a cup and walks with an unsteady gait. Patient 2 struggles to start walking, moves slowly and has rigid limbs. Which pairing of structures is affected, in order?
questions.e:
C is correct. Cerebellar lesions cause problems with coordination without weakness. Basal ganglia dysfunction causes difficulty initiating movement, slow movement and rigidity without weakness.
A: A motor cortex lesion causes contralateral weakness.
B: This reverses the two.
D: Patient 2 shows parkinsonism from the basal ganglia, and a motor cortex lesion would cause weakness.
High yield: Cerebellum improves accuracy. Basal ganglia control timing and integrate movement.

questions.p: Farah, 52, has right leg weakness with hyperactive reflexes that has worsened steadily over the past 3 weeks. Based on the time course alone, which group of causes belongs at the top of her differential?
questions.e:
A is correct. Onset over days to weeks is subacute, with a differential of inflammation, infection, tumour and toxic causes.
B: Degenerative and hereditary causes are chronic, over many months to years.
C: Stroke, migraine aura and trauma are hyperacute, over seconds to minutes.
D: Inflammation and infection alone are the acute list, over hours to a couple of days.
High yield: Use VITAMINS C&D after localizing to build the full differential.

questions.p: A clerk presents a patient with leg weakness and summarizes the symptoms and examination findings. Following the approach to weakness and lesion differential diagnosis, which step comes next?
questions.e:
D is correct. The approach is: describe the problem, localize the lesion, determine the differential, then plan investigations and management.
A: The differential comes after localization.
B: Rate of onset is part of building the differential, after localization.
C: Planning is the final step.
High yield: Describe, localize, differential, plan.

questions.p:
A patient cannot see objects in the right half of the visual field with either eye. Which of the following lesions would produce this pattern?
i) Left optic tract
ii) Left lateral geniculate nucleus
iii) Left optic radiation
iv) Right optic nerve
questions.e:
B is correct. Right hemifield information from each eye travels in the left optic tract, then the left LGN, left optic radiation and left visual cortex. A lesion anywhere along that route removes the right hemifield in both eyes, as with the occipital lesion in your Week 7 quiz.
A: The left optic radiation carries the same information, so iii is also true.
C: A right optic nerve lesion affects the right eye only.
D: A right optic nerve lesion affects one eye only.
E: Statement iv is false.
High yield: Behind the chiasm, each side carries the opposite hemifield from both eyes.

questions.p: An ophthalmology tutor holds a bright object in the upper left part of a student's visual field. Where on the retina does its image land?
o: Lower left part of the retina
Upper right part of the retina
Upper left part of the retinal surface
Lower right part of the retina
questions.e:
D is correct. The image is inverted and flipped on the back of the retina. Upper becomes lower and left becomes right.
A: This inverts the image but does not flip it.
B: This flips the image but does not invert it.
C: This assumes no inversion or flip.
High yield: Retina, optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, LGN, optic radiation, primary visual cortex.

questions.p: Visual signals from the left eye leave the retina and pass through the optic nerve, optic chiasm and optic tract. Which structure do they reach next?
questions.e:
C is correct. The visual pathway runs retina, optic nerves, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, then primary visual cortex.
A: The basal ganglia integrate movement and are not on the visual pathway.
B: The optic radiation follows the LGN.
D: The primary visual cortex is the final stop.
High yield: The occipital lobe gives meaning to visual stimulation.

questions.p: Two patients have visual field testing. Patient 1 has lost all vision in the right eye, and the left eye has full fields. Patient 2 has lost the left half of the visual field in both eyes. Which pairing of lesion sites fits, in order?
o: Optic chiasm, then left optic radiation
Right optic nerve, then right optic tract
Right optic nerve, then left optic tract
Right optic tract, then right optic nerve
questions.e:
B is correct. A lesion before the chiasm affects one eye only, so Patient 1 has a right optic nerve lesion. Left hemifield information from both eyes runs in the right optic tract, so Patient 2 fits a right tract lesion.
A: A chiasm lesion involves both eyes, and the left radiation carries the right hemifield.
C: The left optic tract carries the right hemifield.
D: This reverses the two.
High yield: One eye affected: in front of the chiasm. Same hemifield in both eyes: behind it.

questions.p: Mrs. Lavoie, 67, is right-hand dominant. After a stroke she follows complex spoken commands correctly but speaks in halting, effortful fragments and struggles to produce words. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.e:
B is correct. She understands language but cannot produce it. Motor or expressive language sits in the inferior frontal lobe of the dominant hemisphere.
A: The occipital lobe handles vision.
C: The parietal lobe handles sensation, orientation and attention, not speech production.
D: The posterior temporal lobe holds receptive language, which is intact here.
High yield: Expressive: inferior frontal. Receptive: posterior temporal.

questions.p: Mr. Osei, 72, speaks fluently after a stroke, but he cannot follow simple spoken instructions and his answers do not match the questions asked. His strength is normal. Which region is most likely affected?
questions.e:
A is correct. Fluent speech with poor understanding is a receptive language problem, which localizes to the posterior temporal lobe of the dominant hemisphere.
B: The cerebellum coordinates speech but does not affect understanding.
C: The inferior frontal lobe holds expressive language, which is preserved here.
D: A motor cortex lesion causes contralateral weakness, and his strength is normal.
High yield: The temporal lobe handles auditory processing, language understanding and memory.

questions.p: Two patients have head injuries. Patient 1 is no longer able to plan his day, solve simple problems or switch flexibly between tasks. Patient 2 loses track of where she is and has trouble attending to time and space. Which lobes are affected, in order?
questions.e:
C is correct. Executive function (planning, problem solving, cognitive flexibility) is frontal. Orientation and attention in time and space are parietal.
A: Temporal handles auditory processing and memory, and occipital handles vision.
B: Orientation and attention in time and space are parietal, not temporal.
D: This reverses the two.
High yield: Frontal: motor, speech production, executive function.

questions.p: Two deep grey matter structures are described. Structure 1 integrates cortical activity into a single movement. Structure 2 is a relay centre that integrates and processes sensory and motor information. Which pairing is correct, in order?
questions.e:
A is correct. The basal ganglia are deep nuclei that integrate cortical activity into a single movement. The thalamus is a relay centre for sensory and motor information.
B: The limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate) handles emotions and memory.
C: This reverses the two.
D: The cerebellum improves movement accuracy and coordination.
High yield: Brain grey matter sits outside (cortex) and in deep nuclei.

questions.p: A student reviews a brain specimen in the anatomy lab. Which statement about brain grey and white matter is correct?
o: White matter lies on the outside of the brain, with grey inside
Grey matter holds the axon tracts linking regions of the CNS
The limbic system is a white matter tract that controls movement
Cortex looks darker from dense neurons and little myelin
questions.e:
D is correct. The cortex is darker because of its density of neurons and paucity of myelin. White matter is lighter because of myelin.
A: In the brain, grey matter is outside and white matter inside. The cord is the reverse.
B: Axon tracts make up white matter. Grey matter holds neuron cell bodies.
C: The limbic system is grey matter (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate) for emotions and memory.
High yield: Cortical neurons are folded into gyri.

questions.p: Which sequence correctly traces a voluntary motor command from the brain to a muscle in the leg?
o: Motor cortex, internal capsule, brainstem, pyramids, ventral grey horn
Motor cortex, internal capsule, pyramids, brainstem, dorsal grey horn
Cerebellum, internal capsule, brainstem, pyramids, ventral grey horn
Motor cortex, brainstem, internal capsule, pyramids, ventral grey horn
questions.e:
A is correct. Motor axons descend from the motor cortex through the internal capsule to the brainstem, cross in the pyramids of the medulla, descend in the cord to the ventral grey horn, then exit to the spinal nerve, peripheral nerve, NMJ and muscle.
B: The pyramids sit in the medulla, part of the brainstem, and motor neurons sit in the ventral grey horn.
C: Movement is planned in the motor cortex. The cerebellum refines it through feedback.
D: The internal capsule comes before the brainstem.
High yield: Motor cortex sits in the frontal lobe and plans movement for the contralateral side.

questions.p: A resident explains how movement is refined. Which statement is correct?
o: Cerebellum and basal ganglia loop feedback back to the motor cortex
The cerebellum controls timing and the basal ganglia improve accuracy
The motor cortex sits in the parietal lobe of the brain
Motor axons cross the midline within the internal capsule
questions.e:
A is correct. Input from the cerebellum (improves accuracy) and the basal ganglia (control, integration, timing) loops back to the motor cortex to refine movement.
B: This swaps the two roles.
C: The motor cortex is in the frontal lobe.
D: Motor axons cross in the pyramids of the medulla.
High yield: Neither cerebellar nor basal ganglia lesions cause weakness.

questions.p: Mr. Kowalski, 59, has 6 months of slurred speech, choking on liquids and an unsteady, wide-based gait. Strength is full in all limbs, reflexes are normal and plantar responses are flexor. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.e:
D is correct. The cerebellum coordinates speech, swallowing, limbs and gait. Its lesions cause problems with coordination without weakness.
A: The NMJ affects eyes and swallowing but causes weakness, and strength is full here.
B: A motor cortex lesion causes contralateral weakness with UMN signs.
C: Basal ganglia problems cause slowness, rigidity or excess movement, not loss of coordination of speech and gait.
High yield: Chronic course: think degenerative or hereditary.

questions.p: Mrs. Ito, 61, has developed brief, involuntary, dance-like jerks of her limbs. Strength, reflexes and coordination testing are normal. Which statement about the most likely site of dysfunction is correct?
o: It causes the wide-based gait seen with poor coordination
It sits in the occipital lobe and limbic system
It also causes slowness and rigidity in other patients
It causes contralateral weakness with brisk reflexes
questions.e:
C is correct. Excessive movements such as chorea come from basal ganglia dysfunction. The same structures cause difficulty initiating movement, slowness and rigidity (parkinsonism). Neither pattern includes weakness.
A: Poor coordination of gait is cerebellar.
B: The basal ganglia are deep nuclei, not occipital or limbic structures.
D: Basal ganglia dysfunction does NOT cause weakness.
High yield: Basal ganglia excess movements: chorea, dystonia, athetosis, hemiballismus.

questions.p: Ms. Brandt, 45, has double vision and difficulty swallowing. She also has weakness of the right arm and leg with hyperactive reflexes and an extensor plantar response on the right. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.e:
D is correct. The brainstem houses all cranial nerve nuclei and carries the motor tracts. Cranial nerve signs plus UMN limb signs place the lesion there.
A: Cerebellar lesions do not cause weakness.
B: A cord lesion spares the cranial nerves.
C: The NMJ affects eyes and swallowing, but the brisk reflexes and extensor plantar are UMN signs.
High yield: Eyes and swallowing with LMN signs: NMJ. With UMN signs: brainstem.

questions.p: A small stroke damages Mr. Ruiz's right thalamus. Both the dorsal column and the spinothalamic pathways pass through it. Which sensory loss is expected?
o: Left side pain, with right side vibration
Right side, for vibration and for pain
Left side, for vibration and for pain
Right side pain, with left side vibration
questions.e:
C is correct. The spinothalamic tract crosses at entry to the cord and the dorsal column crosses in the medulla. By the thalamus, both carry the opposite side of the body, so a right thalamic lesion affects all modalities on the left.
A: This split pattern only arises in the spinal cord, before the dorsal column crosses.
B: Both tracts have crossed below the thalamus.
D: This split also needs a cord lesion, on the opposite side.
High yield: Sensory pathway: nerves, roots, cord, brainstem, thalamus, white matter, primary sensory cortex.

questions.p: A patient has right-sided weakness with hyperactive reflexes, spasticity and an extensor plantar response. Which additional finding most specifically places this UMN lesion in the brain rather than the spinal cord?
o: Absence of muscle atrophy on the right side
questions.e:
A is correct. Language lives in the frontal and temporal lobes, so language impairment places a UMN lesion in the brain. Neglect is another brain clue.
B: Absent fasciculations is a general UMN sign.
C: Absent atrophy is a general UMN sign and does not separate brain from cord.
D: Hyperactive reflexes are a general UMN sign found with brain or cord lesions.
High yield: More specific UMN clues: language impairment, neglect, bladder symptoms.

questions.p: Two patients present with left arm weakness. Patient 1's weakness came on over a few seconds while gardening. Patient 2's weakness has crept up slowly over 2 years, and her mother had a similar illness. Which time-course category and leading cause fits each, in order?
o: Acute infection, then subacute tumour growth
questions.e:
B is correct. Seconds to minutes is hyperacute, which includes stroke. Many months to years is chronic, which includes degenerative and hereditary causes. The family history favours hereditary.
A: Nothing suggests trauma, and 2 years is chronic, not subacute.
C: Stroke is hyperacute, not chronic.
D: Acute is hours to days, and subacute is days to weeks.
High yield: Hyperacute: stroke, migraine aura, trauma. Chronic: degenerative, hereditary.

questions.p: Mr. Bianchi, 78, has 8 months of a shuffling gait disturbance, new urinary incontinence and worsening memory. He takes no anticoagulants and has no cancer history. What is the most appropriate next step and the structural concern?
o: MoCA only, as imaging is reserved for age under 60
No imaging, as this is a typical slow memory decline
Neuroimaging, for hydrocephalus from blocked CSF flow
Neuroimaging, for a lesion of the occipital lobe
questions.e:
C is correct. Gait disturbance with urinary incontinence suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus, an indication for neuroimaging. Hydrocephalus results when CSF flow through the ventricles is blocked.
A: Age under 60 is one indication. NPH is a separate one.
B: Gait disturbance with incontinence is not typical memory decline.
D: The occipital lobe handles vision, which is not affected here.
High yield: BRAIN: bleeding risk, abnormal presentation, intracranial lesion, NPH.
